method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Examine repeatedly** to catch persisting or evolving signs and to judge response to treatment.
claims.source_text: Repeated examination is useful to identify the persistence or evolution of signs, and evaluate response to treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Give appropriate analgesia — it will not mask potentially serious causes of pain.**
claims.source_text: Appropriate analgesia should be used and will not mask potentially serious causes of pain
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most children do not need investigations**; choose tests by the most likely cause.
claims.source_text: Investigations are guided by the most likely cause. Most children do not need investigations
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Appendicitis in young children may be atypical** and can present as sepsis or perforation.
claims.source_text: Appendicitis in young children may not present with classic symptoms and can present as sepsis or perforation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The key task is separating conditions that need specific or urgent — especially surgical — management** from the common self-limited ones (gastroenteritis, constipation, viral illness). Check for red flags before labelling pain non-specific.
claims.source_text: Abdominal pain is a common non-specific symptom that is often associated with self-limited conditions such as gastroenteritis, constipation and viral illness … The key consideration in acute abdominal pain is the differentiation between conditions which require specific or urgent management, particularly surgical management … Non-specific abdominal pain is common. Assess for red flags for other causes prior to making this diagnosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Neonates** may show symptoms that parents read as abdominal pain — **examine thoroughly and keep a broad differential.** Infants may present only with crying, irritability, poor feeding, lethargy, drawing up the legs or refusing to weight bear.
claims.source_text: Symptoms in neonates may be attributed by parents as abdominal pain. A thorough examination and a broad differential should be considered in this group … Neonates and infants may present with persistent crying, irritability, poor feeding and lethargy, draw up legs, refusal to weight bear
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Appendicitis under 5 years** is often diagnosed late and may be atypical: fever, vomiting and pain, perforation or sepsis, or diarrhoea mimicking gastroenteritis. **It needs careful fluid and antibiotic management.**
claims.source_text: Appendicitis in young children <5 years old Often diagnosed late in the course of illness May not present with classical symptoms Presentation often includes fever, vomiting, abdominal pain perforation or sepsis diarrhea mimicking gastroenteritis Requires careful attention to fluid and antibiotic management.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pain character clues:** sudden onset — testicular or ovarian torsion/rupture, intussusception, volvulus, perforated viscus, incarcerated hernia. **Bilious vomiting** — volvulus or obstruction.
claims.source_text: Sudden onset Testicular or ovarian torsion/rupture Intussusception Volvulus Perforated viscus Incarcerated hernia … Bilious vomiting Volvulus Obstruction
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hirschsprung enterocolitis** presents with sudden painful distension and bloody diarrhoea; these children can deteriorate rapidly and risk colonic perforation.
claims.source_text: Hirschsprung disease Enterocolitis presents with sudden painful abdominal distension and bloody diarrhoea. children can rapidly deteriorate with dehydration, electrolyte disturbances and systemic toxicity and are at risk of colonic perforation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Palpate for** focal vs generalised tenderness, percussion (then rebound) tenderness, guarding or rigidity, masses and faeces. **Serial examination is required. Examine the genitalia** (e.g. for testicular torsion).
claims.source_text: Palpate for focal vs generalized tenderness percussion tenderness and, if negative, rebound tenderness* guarding or rigidity* abdominal masses palpable faeces Serial examination of the abdomen is required Examine genitalia eg for testicular torsion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Rectal or vaginal examination is rarely indicated**; discuss with a senior clinician first, and if needed do it only once.
claims.source_text: Rectal or vaginal examination is rarely indicated in a child, this should be discussed with a senior clinician and if needed, should only be performed once
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Peritonism:** the child won't move in bed, can't walk or hop comfortably, and has percussion tenderness; internal rotation of the right hip can irritate an inflamed appendix.
claims.source_text: Children will often not want to move in the bed and will be unable to walk or hop comfortably, and will have abdominal tenderness with percussion, internal rotation of the right hip can irritate an inflamed appendix
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Targeted tests** may include urinalysis (± culture ± pregnancy test), LFTs, lipase, venous gas for lactate/acidosis, glucose for DKA, and FBE/CRP (± ESR).
claims.source_text: Urine analysis (+/- culture +/- pregnancy test if indicated) LFTs eg for hepatitis Lipase eg for pancreatitis Venous blood gas for lactate/acidosis Blood glucose for DKA … FBE and CRP (+/- ESR) eg for inflammatory/infectious cause such as inflammatory bowel disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **AXR only if obstruction is suspected** — it does not help diagnose constipation. CXR if pneumonia is suspected.
claims.source_text: AXR if obstruction suspected. It is not helpful in diagnosing constipation CXR if pneumonia is suspected
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ultrasound after senior discussion** — very low yield if used indiscriminately. ⚠️ **Not indicated in the initial assessment of testicular torsion; it may delay time-critical surgery.** Useful for suspected ovarian torsion and when the history suggests intussusception, even with a normal examination.
claims.source_text: Ultrasound may be requested after discussion with a senior clinician (very low yield if used indiscriminately) … It is not clinically indicated in the initial assessment for testicular torsion and may delay time critical surgery. May be requested after discussion with surgeons Useful in suspected ovarian torsion Useful if the history is suggestive of intussusception, even if examination is normal
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severe pain: IV morphine or intranasal fentanyl may be needed as initial analgesia.** Fluid resuscitation may be required.
claims.source_text: Fluid resuscitation may be required (see Intravenous fluids) Provide adequate analgesia. IV morphine or intranasal fentanyl may be required as initial analgesia in severe pain
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider fasting** depending on the differential; **give enteral or IV fluids if assessment or diagnosis is delayed** (e.g. 4 hours if very young).
claims.source_text: Consider fasting, depending on differential diagnosis. Consider enteral or intravenous fluids if assessment or diagnosis is delayed, eg 4 hours if very young
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer early** if a surgical or gynaecological diagnosis is possible; **consider a nasogastric tube** if bowel obstruction is suspected.
claims.source_text: Early referral of children with possible diagnoses requiring surgical or gynaecological management Consider a nasogastric tube if bowel obstruction is suspected
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Involve the paediatric team** when a surgical cause is suspected, or with severe pain, peritonism, bilious vomiting, scrotal pain/redness and swelling, or if admission is needed.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when Surgical cause suspected Severe pain Signs of peritonism Bilious vomiting Scrotal pain/redness and swelling Child requiring admission
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Before transferring a child with a possible surgical condition**, ensure adequate analgesia, venous access and IV fluids.
claims.source_text: Prior to transferring infants or children with possible surgical conditions, ensure the child has adequate analgesia, venous access and intravenous fluids
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when** there are no concerning features, the picture fits non-specific abdominal pain, a clear follow-up plan exists (e.g. GP) and parents know when to return.
claims.source_text: Consider discharge when There are no concerning clinical features Presentation consistent with non-specific abdominal pain … A clear follow-up plan has been arranged, eg with local GP Parents have been given advice regarding when to seek medical attention
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Abdominal pain - acute' (Last updated April 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Abdominal_pain_-_acute/, retrieved 2026-09-23
